notes:
Below is a verse-by-verse commentary on Deuteronomy 25 drawn from the traditional commentaries and study resources that were accessible.

---

## Deuteronomy 25 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### vv. 1–3: Corporal Punishment Limited to Forty Lashes

**v. 1: “If there is a dispute between men, they are to go to court to be judged, so that the innocent may be acquitted and the guilty condemned.”**

The Pulpit Commentary notes that verses 1–2 should be read as a single sentence: the *protasis* (the “if” clause) is in v. 1 and the *apodosis* (the “then” clause) follows in v. 2. It is assumed the judges will pronounce a just verdict — “justify the righteous and condemn the wicked” — and then the manner of punishment is prescribed. The beating was usually administered with a stick (Ex 21:10; 2 Sam 7:14), though sometimes thorns (Judg 8:7,16) or scourges with sharp points (1 Kgs 12:11,14) were used. The culprit was laid on the ground and struck on the back and shoulders (Prov 10:13; 19:29; 26:3; Isa 1:6).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

Ellicott highlights that “justify” is used here *forensically* — not meaning “to make righteous” but “to treat as righteous.” He adds: “Those who object to this sense in St. Paul’s Epistles will find it hard to put any other sense upon the word in the rest of Holy Scripture.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic/Pentecostal-leaning) says: “By the direction of God, Israel’s legal system made the distinction between criminal cases … and civil cases. … When the righteous are penalized and the guilty are rewarded, courts of justice are not fulfilling their God-given responsibility (Romans 13:4).”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

Precept Austin adds that “dispute” (Hebrew *rib*) describes a quarrel, lawsuit, or contention. “Justify” (Hebrew *tsadeq*) means to declare right, acquit, or treat as innocent. “Condemn” (Hebrew *rasha*) means to declare guilty or wicked. Legal cases in Israel were meant to prevent personal revenge.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-25-commentary

**v. 2: “If the guilty man deserves to be beaten, the judge shall have him lie down and be flogged in his presence with the number of lashes his crime warrants.”**

Keil & Delitzsch explain the Hebrew idiom *“son of stripes”* — i.e., a man liable to be beaten. The punishment had to be administered “in the presence of the judge,” who oversaw it to ensure justice. The number of blows was to be “according to the need of his crime in number” — proportionate to the offense.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-25.html (snippet)

Ellicott notes that the Talmudic treatise *Makkoth* describes later practice: the man was made to incline his body (not fully lying down), and the thirty-nine stripes were given: thirteen on one shoulder, thirteen on the other, and thirteen on the breast. The punishment was administered in the synagogue while passages from Deuteronomy 28:58–59 were read.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

Guzik adds: “A beating was the appropriate punishment, yet God’s law also recognized that punishment could be excessive, and therefore gave limits.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

**v. 3: “He may receive no more than forty lashes, lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight.”**

The Pulpit Commentary says the number forty was probably chosen for its symbolic significance as the “measure of completeness” in judgment (cf. Gen 7:12; Num 14:33–34). The rabbis later fixed the number at thirty-nine to guard against accidentally exceeding forty. Maimonides gives an additional reason: the scourge had three thongs, each stroke counting as three; thus thirteen strokes made thirty-nine — to give forty would require a fourteenth stroke, exceeding the limit.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

Gill’s Exposition notes that Paul received “forty stripes save one” five times (2 Cor 11:24), confirming the Jewish custom of giving only thirty-nine. The scourge of three lashes meant thirteen strikes delivered thirty-nine blows. The Talmud also required assessing what the man could physically bear, and the punishment could be divided if necessary.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/25-3.htm

Guzik points out the motive clause: “*lest your brother be degraded in your sight.*” God commanded that the dignity of even the guilty man be respected. Quoting Eugene Merrill: “His sinful conduct against a brother was not sufficient cause to rob him of his full dignity.” G. Campbell Morgan is cited: “It is interesting to notice what excessive punishment is to the mind of God. It is anything which makes our brother appear vile in our sight.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

Precept Austin echoes this: “Even in punishment a humanitarian spirit prevails. Restoration and changed character are always the goal.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-25-commentary

---

### v. 4: Do Not Muzzle the Ox

**v. 4: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.”**

The Pulpit Commentary explains that in ancient threshing, an ox walked over the grain to separate it from the husk. The law permitted the animal to eat freely as it worked. “This prohibition, therefore, was dictated by a regard to the rights and claims of animals employed in labor; but there is involved in it the general principle that all labor is to be duly requited.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

Ellicott observes that Paul comments on this verse twice (1 Cor 9:9 and 1 Tim 5:18): “It is not only written for the sake of the oxen, but to prove that the ‘labourer is worthy of his hire;’ ‘they that preach the Gospel should live of the Gospel.’”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

Guzik notes that Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:9–10 even asks, “Is it oxen God is concerned about? Or does He say it altogether for our sakes?” — suggesting the application to ministers was the deeper point.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

Precept Austin cites Kline: “The positive counterpart to the prohibition of dishonoring a man in spite of his evil works is the requirement that he receive all proper honor for his good works.” It also cites Utley: Paul uses a rabbinical method of “lesser to greater” (*qal wa-ḥomer*): if true for oxen, how much more for human laborers.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-25-commentary

**Denominational note — use of this verse for pastoral support:** Across Protestant traditions, this verse (via Paul’s application) is used to support the principle that ministers/elders should be financially supported by the church. The Reformed tradition (see ligonier.org and thegospelcoalition.org) and Baptist traditions (see desiringgod.org) both affirm this. The Lutheran tradition (LCMS, 1517.org) also upholds it. There is no major *doctrinal* divide over this verse; differences, if any, are practical — e.g., whether a “tent-making” ministry model (self-supporting) is equally valid, or whether full-time paid ministry is the biblical norm. Paul himself modeled both.

---

### vv. 5–10: Levirate Marriage

**v. 5: “When brothers dwell together and one of them dies without a son, the widow must not marry outside the family. Her husband’s brother is to take her as his wife and fulfill the duty of a brother-in-law for her.”**

This is the law of *levirate marriage* (from Latin *levir*, “brother-in-law”). The Pulpit Commentary notes that the custom predates Moses (see Gen 38:8, Judah and Tamar) and existed among other ancient peoples. Its purpose was to prevent a family from becoming extinct and its property from passing to strangers.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

Ellicott adds that the law is the subject of an entire Talmudic tractate (*Yebâmôth*). The object was achieved if the family of the dead man was perpetuated; the marriage did not have to be between the brother and the widow specifically but could involve other representatives (see Ruth 4).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

Precept Austin, citing the NET Bible notes, explains that this is “the only reference to this practice in an OT legal text but it is illustrated in the story of Judah and his sons (Gen 38) and possibly in the account of Ruth and Boaz.” Utley notes the whole purpose was “to keep the inheritance within the family.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-25-commentary

Guzik cites Thompson: the practice “was not peculiar to Israel, for it was practiced among the Hittites and Assyrians as well as in countries such as India, Africa and South America.” Kalland is quoted: “Was the law of levirate marriage an approval of polygamy? Hardly! It was rather an alternate arrangement under specific bounds to make possible the retention of landed property throughout the families of Israel.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

**v. 6: “The first son she bears will carry on the name of the dead brother, so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel.”**

The Pulpit Commentary explains the phrase “shall succeed in the name of his brother” (literally “shall rise up on the name”) means the firstborn would be enrolled in the family register as the heir of the deceased and perpetuate his name.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

Guzik notes that “son” (*ben*) may simply mean “child.” Kalland is cited: “Moses had already established that when no male heir existed, daughters would be heirs of their father’s property (Num 27:1–8).” This interpretation is supported by the LXX, Josephus, and the Rabbis.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

**v. 7: “But if the man does not want to marry his brother’s widow, she is to go to the elders at the city gate and say, ‘My husband’s brother refuses to preserve his brother’s name in Israel…’”**

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the man was free to refuse; the marriage was not absolutely compulsory. But the widow had recourse: she could bring the matter before the elders at the city gate (the place of judgment).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

**v. 8: “Then the elders of his city shall summon him and speak with him. If he persists and says, ‘I do not want to marry her,’”**

The elders were first to try persuasion. Only if the man “stood firm” did the shame ceremony proceed.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

**v. 9: “…his brother’s widow shall go up to him in the presence of the elders, remove his sandal, spit in his face, and declare, ‘This is what is done to the man who will not maintain his brother’s line.’”**

The Pulpit Commentary explains the sandal removal as an act of indignity: the shod foot planted on property symbolised possession (Ps 60:8; 108:9), so the forcible removal of the sandal indicated contemptuous rejection and repudiation of rights. To walk barefoot was considered ignominious (Isa 20:2,4; 2 Sam 15:30). The spitting was understood by Jewish interpreters as spitting *on the ground before his face*, not directly on it. Even this, by Eastern standards, was deeply insulting (cf. Num 12:14).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

Precept Austin elaborates: the sandal ritual was “a symbol of the renunciation of a man’s position and property (cf. Ruth 4:7–8).” The refusal brother was “deprived of the position which he ought to have occupied.”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-25-commentary

**v. 10: “And his family name in Israel will be called ‘The House of the Unsandaled.’”**

Guzik notes that this public disgrace and permanent label shows how seriously Israel took family responsibility. The Ruth 4 narrative uses the sandal removal but notably omits the spitting.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

Ellicott observes that the Sadducees later raised a question on this law to Jesus about the resurrection (Matt 22:23–33). He comments: “It is worth while to observe that the law itself demands that in some sense there should be a resurrection. … Why should the name of the dead be kept up, if the dead has passed out of existence?”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

---

### vv. 11–12: The Wife Who Grabs a Man’s Genitals

**v. 11: “If two men are fighting, and the wife of one steps in to rescue her husband from the one striking him, and she reaches out her hand and grabs his genitals,”**

The Pulpit Commentary says that although the childless widow was permitted to approach a man (in the levirate context), no license was granted to women to pass beyond the bounds of decency in their approaches to the other sex. Hence this severe prohibition.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

Ellicott calls this “another precept of humanity” and the counterpart to Exodus 21:22 (which protects a pregnant woman from harm during a fight). He says the precept is meant “to enforce modesty as well as to protect humanity.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

**v. 12: “you are to cut off her hand. You must show her no pity.”**

Guzik explains that the punishment followed the *lex talionis* (eye-for-eye) principle: “She had mutilated a man, ruining his ability to father children. Her body would also be mutilated by the amputation of her hand, the part of her body that committed the offense.” Thompson is cited: “Possibly it was representative of similar offenses and provided a standard for judgment in all such cases. Perhaps also, the law arose from the desire to protect the reproductive organs and thus obviate anything that might prevent a man leaving descendants.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the rabbis later commuted this sentence into a fine equal to the value of the hand.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

---

### vv. 13–16: Honest Weights and Measures

**v. 13: “You shall not have two differing weights in your bag, one heavy and one light.”**

The Pulpit Commentary explains the Hebrew “a stone and a stone” — a large weight for buying (to get more from the seller) and a small one for selling (to give less to the buyer). This echoes Amos 8:5.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

**v. 14: “You shall not have two differing measures in your house, one large and one small.”**

The same principle applied to measures (an ephah for dry goods).

**v. 15: “You must maintain accurate and honest weights and measures, so that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.”**

Guzik says: “God commanded that His people do business honestly. … The surrounding culture may believe that it doesn’t matter if money is made ethically or not, but God commands a perfect and just weight.” Merrill is cited: “There obviously was no sin in possessing these things per se, but their very possession would inevitably lead to their use in unscrupulous transactions.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

The long-life promise attached to this command is the same covenant blessing attached to the fifth commandment (Deut 5:16; 4:26).

**v. 16: “For everyone who behaves dishonestly in regard to these things is detestable to the LORD your God.”**

Ellicott notes that the chief practical concern was protection of the poor: “Rich men can take care of themselves. Poor men are doubly robbed by short weight and measure, because they cannot protect themselves against it. The injustice tends to perpetuate their poverty.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

Precept Austin cross-references Proverbs 11:1 (“a false balance is abomination to the LORD”) and Amos 8:4–8.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-25-commentary

Guzik summarises: “Stealing from others under the cover of doing business is a serious crime before God.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

---

### vv. 17–19: Remember Amalek

**v. 17: “Remember what the Amalekites did to you along your way from Egypt,”**

The Pulpit Commentary frames this as a sharp contrast: while brotherly love was to govern relations within Israel, the enemies of God and His people were to be overcome by force — wickedness was to be removed by the extinction of the wicked.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

**v. 18: “how they met you on your journey when you were tired and weary, and they attacked all your stragglers; they had no fear of God.”**

The Pulpit Commentary highlights the rare Hebrew verb *zinnēb* (“and tailed thee,” i.e., cut off thy tail/rear), a denominative from *zānāv* (tail). It appears only here and in Joshua 10:19. The Amalekites attacked the stragglers — the faint, weary, and feeble at the rear.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/25.htm

Ellicott observes that these details about attacking the hindmost are *not* given in the Exodus 17 account. Amalek’s attack came after the water from the rock at Horeb; the faint and weary naturally stayed behind at the water, and there the Amalekites “cruelly massacred them.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

Guzik notes: the Amalekites descended from Esau (Gen 36:15–16). Thompson is quoted: “Amalek’s failure to show mercy to the weak merited divine judgment, for God judged nations for crimes against natural law.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

**v. 19: “When the LORD your God gives you rest from the enemies around you in the land that He is giving you to possess as an inheritance, you are to blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. Do not forget!”**

Ellicott traces the stages of this command’s fulfillment: it was entrusted first to Joshua (Ex 17:14), then carried out by Barak and Gideon (Judg 5:14; 6:3; 7:12), Saul and Samuel (1 Sam 15), David (1 Sam 27:8–9; 30:17), the Simeonites (1 Chr 4:42–43), and finally by Esther’s extermination of the Agagites (Haman’s line).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

Guzik notes that Saul’s failure to destroy Amalek fully was the primary act of disobedience that cost him the throne (1 Sam 15:2–9; 28:18). Many interpreters see Amalek typologically: “Israel’s struggle with Amalek as a picture of the believer’s struggle with the flesh, which constantly battles against the spirit and must be struggled against until completely conquered (Gal 5:17).” Clarke is cited: “It is supposed that this command had its final accomplishment in the death of Haman and his ten sons, Esther 3, 7, 9.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-25/

---

## Denominational Perspectives and Other Views

### Justification Language (v. 1)

Ellicott makes a pointed theological observation: the verb “justify” in Deuteronomy 25:1 is used *forensically* — treating someone as righteous, not making them righteous. He notes that “those who object to this sense in St. Paul’s Epistles will find it hard to put any other sense upon the word in the rest of Holy Scripture.” This is significant for the **Reformed and Lutheran** traditions, which insist on forensic (declarative) justification. The same Hebrew verb *tsadeq* undergirds both Old and New Testament usage.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/25.htm

### Levirate Marriage and the Resurrection (vv. 5–10)

Ellicott notes that the Sadducees used this law to question Jesus about the resurrection (Matt 22:23–33). He remarks that “the law itself demands that in some sense there should be a resurrection,” since preserving a dead man’s name only makes sense if the dead continue to exist. This is a reading shared broadly across Protestant and Catholic traditions. The **Catholic** reading (see the *Catena Aurea* and patristic commentaries on Matthew 22 at newadvent.org) focuses on Jesus’ answer that in the resurrection people “neither marry nor are given in marriage,” affirming both the reality of the resurrection and the temporary, earthly nature of levirate marriage.

### The Ox Muzzle and Ministerial Support (v. 4)

The apostle Paul’s use of this verse in 1 Corinthians 9:9–10 and 1 Timothy 5:18 is universally recognised across Protestant traditions. The **Reformed** tradition (e.g., Calvin, cited at monergism.com) emphasises that the *spiritual* application is the primary one — God’s care for oxen points to His greater care for ministers of the gospel. **Baptist** teachers (e.g., John Piper at desiringgod.org) likewise use this verse to argue that congregations should generously support those who labour in preaching and teaching. The **Pentecostal/charismatic** reading (e.g., Enduring Word) affirms the same principle. No major doctrinal divide exists on this verse.

### The Destruction of Amalek (vv. 17–19)

The command to “blot out the memory of Amalek” has occasioned discussion about divine judgment and the morality of herem (devotion to destruction). The **Reformed** tradition typically sees this as an act of divine justice through a covenant nation, not as a precedent for holy war by the church (which wields spiritual, not carnal, weapons). **Baptist** and **evangelical** readings (e.g., at gty.org, desiringgod.org) tend to emphasise Amalek’s sin and God’s patience (over 400 years passed before Saul was commissioned) as well as the typological application to the believer’s war against indwelling sin. **Modern scholarship** (e.g., bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes) tends to treat the Amalekite command within its ancient Near Eastern context of total warfare and questions its compatibility with New Testament ethics of enemy-love.

---

*Sources consulted: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Precept Austin, Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott’s Commentary for English Readers, Gill’s Exposition, Keil & Delitzsch, and associated cross-references. All URLs are cited at the relevant points above.*
